titulo.texto: Mural of the Tzompantli of Human Diversity

frase_gancho.texto: Skulls that teach us to read the human body as a story.

puente_narrativo.texto: Now the journey truly begins: continue to Hall 2 and see how the first settlers reached the Americas, following the tracks of the great animals of the Pleistocene.

guion_corto.texto: Here there are skulls, and they are not a macabre decoration: they are a way of reading the human body as if it were a book. Notice that they do not all have the same shape. In ancient Mexico, some communities shaped babies’ heads with small boards and bandages, to give them an elongated form that was a sign of beauty or of belonging to a group. Teeth were also filed, and sometimes stones such as jade were set into them. But what matters most is what does not change: beneath all those differences, every skull belongs to the same species. That is the lesson of this hall: very different on the outside; almost identical on the inside.

guion_largo.texto:
To understand this corner of the hall, it helps to know what a Tzompantli is. It was a wooden structure where the Mexica strung the skulls of sacrificial victims, as an offering to the gods and as a warning of their power. A few years ago, archaeologists discovered a monumental one next to the Templo Mayor. Here the museum looks at that image with the opposite intention: not to honor the gods through death, but to show how much we resemble one another and how, even so, each people inscribed itself on the body.

There is a phrase that sums up physical anthropology: the body is also history. From the bones, one can tell whether a person was a man or a woman, how many years they lived, what they ate, what illnesses they suffered, and even whether they went hungry as a girl, because tooth enamel keeps those traces. And, at times, also how they wanted to look. That last part is the most fascinating. In many Mesoamerican cultures, especially among the Maya, babies’ heads were bound with small boards during the first weeks, when the bone is still soft, so that the forehead would grow longer. It was not a punishment: it was an ideal of beauty, and sometimes of nobility. If you look at the profile of [Pakal](mna_s09_mascara_pakal) in the Maya Hall, with the nose that seems to continue straight up into the forehead, you are looking at exactly that standard.

Something similar happened with teeth. Some people filed them into decorative shapes, and others had small discs of jade or pyrite set into their incisors. Imagine smiling with a bright green stone: it was a sign of rank and of identity. And there are also skulls with trepanations, openings made with stone instruments; in some, the bone shows signs of healing, which means the patient survived the operation.

All of this goes hand in hand with an idea that is the backbone of the museum. During the nineteenth century and much of the twentieth, there were those who classified humanity into “races” and ranked them in hierarchies, using skull measurements as a pretext. Today science knows otherwise: our species was born in Africa about two hundred or three hundred thousand years ago, spread across the entire planet, and acquired differences in skin color, hair form, or height in response to the sun, the cold, and the diet of each place. Genetic variation within a single people is usually greater than the variation between one people and another. Put simply: we are one single family.

Think of it as one thread: [Lucy](mna_s01_lucy_afarensis) is the beginning, the [three young people from the burial](mna_s01_entierro_dolni_vestonice) you have just seen are people like you, and these skulls are the diversity that came afterward. When you finish here, take that way of looking with you. In every hall you will see bodies shaped, adorned, and painted. The Olmec, with baby faces. The Maya, with elongated foreheads. The Teotihuacán, with stone masks. Upstairs, in the ethnography halls, there are living people who still adorn themselves today with ribbons, feathers, and fabrics. The human body has always been a canvas, and it is up to you to read it.

texto.Culture: Museum display on the biological diversity of Homo sapiens
texto.Origin: Introduction to Anthropology Hall, National Museum of Anthropology, Mexico City

texto.pregunta: Myth: The skulls in this hall are war trophies of the Aztecs.
texto.respuesta: Reality: They are here for scientific purposes, to show how the human body varies and what body modification customs existed; they are not trophies.
